transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-12-18
Time: 14:00 - 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~60 minutes
Attendees: Alex Martin (Redwood AE), Priya Rao (Redwood SE), Tom Jenkins (Lighthouse CTO), Maya Lopez (Lead ML Eng), Rashid Khan (Infra Eng)

Summary:
Quick deep dive on p95/p99 tail latency for Lighthouse's inference workload. Focus areas: streaming vs non-streaming, network hops (VPC peering vs public egress), KV cache behavior and hit rates, batching/autoscaling and quantization tradeoffs for 8-bit/4-bit. Action items and pilot next steps agreed.

Topics covered:
- Measurement methodology: where to measure (client vs edge vs model runtime), synthetic vs production traces
- KV cache: warm vs cold start, sharding, cache hit rate impact on tail
- Batching and continuous batching behavior with bursty traffic
- Streaming vs non-streaming p95/p99 differences and when streaming helps
- Network topology: VPC peering, cross-AZ hops, firewall/NAT timeouts
- Quantization and its perf/quality tradeoffs on tail latency
- Practical mitigations: pre-warming, prioritized routing, fallback model variants

Transcript:
[00:00] Alex Martin: hey everyone, thanks for joining, i'm alex from Redwood, i'm the AE on this account. we brought Priya who is our system engineer to walk through the runtime behavior. how's everything on your side?
[00:12] Tom Jenkins: good, thanks. we've got Maya and Rashid on for the infra and model sides. looking forward to digging into our p99s. we've been seeing some spikes around peak usage, looks like 600ms -> 2.3s p99 depending on prompt length.
[00:27] Priya Rao: cool, yeah we'll try to get to root cause today. quick question, are those numbers measured at your client (frontend) or are they Redwood API observed?
[00:36] Maya Lopez: measured at our frontend CDN logs, so includes network + ssl + our app processing. we also pulled Redwood's reported metrics which are ~1.1s p99 for similar traces. so there's a delta.
[00:48] Priya Rao: that delta is important. p95/p99 are often dominated by network hops, retransmits, cold kv cache, and scheduling. we'll break it down.
[00:57] [00:57] Rashid Khan: and we're using VPC peering into Redwood Dedicated, with the peering across accounts and a transit VPC, so there are a couple network hops.
[01:07] Priya Rao: ok noted, cross-account peering and transit VPC adds a few ms per hop and can amplify jitter. also NAT gateways and firewall proxies sometimes create long tail timeouts on TLS handshakes if connection reuse isn't working.
[01:23] Alex Martin: to frame it, we'll talk about where latency is added: client -> internet -> edge -> control plane -> model runtime. at each stage there are queuing and serialization effects.
[01:34] Maya Lopez: we mainly care about user perceived p99 for short-chat prompts (avg 80 tokens) and longer generation (200 tokens). streaming is enabled for chat.
[01:44] Priya Rao: ok streaming vs non-streaming difference: streaming reduces time-to-first-token, and can mask tail on long outputs because the early tokens arrive while the backend finishes other work. however streaming doesn't reduce tail of final token when the model stalls on compute or cache misses.
[02:01] [02:01] Tom Jenkins: interesting, we saw p99 improve for UX when we switched to streaming for chat, but our observability still shows tail spikes in completions for large multi-turn prompts.
[02:12] Priya Rao: that suggests KV cache cold misses or cache fragmentation. for multi-turn, if the KV cache hit rate drops, we re-run attention from earlier tokens or we fetch KV from colder storage which adds latency spikes.
[02:25] Rashid Khan: is KV cache shared across GPUs in your Dedicated setup? we have a shard per GPU model and we run multiple model replicas. sometimes requests get routed off-shard.
[02:34] Priya Rao: by default Redwood keeps KV cache local to the serving replica to avoid cross-GPU network traffic. we use a smart routing policy to keep sticky sessions when possible, but routing can change during autoscaling or failovers which causes cold cache on the new replica.
[02:49] Alex Martin: that sticky behavior is tunable; you can pin sessions or use a warm pool to reduce re-routing.
[02:56] Maya Lopez: we have a pretty bursty pattern: big batch at 9am, mid-day spikes, then small background requests. what would you recommend for batching strategy? we tried larger batch sizes but saw latency regressions.
[03:09] Priya Rao: continuous batching helps for throughput but increases head-of-line wait for low-latency requests. we support service-level policies: low-latency routes (small max batch, preemptive execution) and cost routes (bigger batching). for p99 tail you often want a hybrid: prioritize small requests, and use batching for background/async jobs.
[03:26] Tom Jenkins: how about quantization? we've tried 8-bit on dev and saw small quality regressions but big perf wins on average latency. does quantization affect tail?
[03:36] Priya Rao: quant improves throughput and can reduce median latency, but tail behavior is nuanced. if quantized kernels saturate GPU memory less, autoscaling reacts differently; also certain kernels have variable performance at extremes—some quant implementations can have jitter for certain sequence lengths. we recommend per-model profiling — Redwood Optimize suggests quantization profiles by workload.
[03:57] [03:57] Rashid Khan: network timeouts — we see occasional TLS renegotiation causing 200-600ms spikes. any best practices?
[04:06] Priya Rao: reusing keep-alive connections and using gRPC or HTTP/2 with multiplexing reduces handshake spikes. also ensure your NAT and LB idle timeouts align with client keepalive. we can share a suggested tcp/tls tuning doc.
[04:18] Alex Martin: also instrument at the client to capture tcp_rtt, ssl handshake time, and Redwood request start vs finish to separate network vs runtime tail.
[04:27] Maya Lopez: on measuring p95/p99, should we compute on user-perceived latencies or backend-only?
[04:33] Priya Rao: both. user-perspective p99 is what matters for UX; backend p99 helps you root cause. typically we ask for both traces side-by-side and align timestamps to see where the delta sits.
[04:44] [04:44] Tom Jenkins: about autoscaling: during a sudden spike we saw new nodes spin up but request latency spiked for 30-40s. what's happening?
[04:53] Priya Rao: common pattern — traffic hits and the autoscaler creates new replicas, but until the new replica warms its KV cache and model weights are loaded (or until it hits steady-state), requests routed there see cold-start penalties. we use warm pools and pre-warmed containers to mitigate this. you can also configure gradual scale policies to avoid mass re-routing.
[05:11] Rashid Khan: can pre-warming fully eliminate the cold-start p99?
[05:15] Priya Rao: it reduces it significantly but not fully—there are still potential network or OS-level jitter. pre-warm gives better 99th percentile but keep in mind load balancer stickiness and draining behaviors.
[05:26] Maya Lopez: ok let's talk about streaming again. for our chat UI, time-to-first-token matters a lot. you said streaming helps. any pitfalls?
[05:33] Priya Rao: streaming improves perceived latency but requires you to handle partial outputs and eventual completion events. also backpressure and chunking strategy matter: smaller chunks mean more frequent network writes—which can increase packets and cause variance. Redwood supports configurable chunk sizes and you can measure tradeoffs.
[05:48] Alex Martin: another tail source is large prompts with many special tokens — tokenizer edge cases can force slower kernels. we recommend profiling by prompt length histogram.
[05:58] [05:58] Tom Jenkins: suggestion — we can share our top 100 prompt templates and frequency distribution.
[06:02] Priya Rao: perfect, that helps. we'll run a bench that replays real traffic and measure backend and e2e p95/p99.
[06:09] Maya Lopez: about VPC/on-prem: if we go private deployment on our VPC, does that remove network hops?
[06:16] Priya Rao: Private deployment (on-prem or VPC/private link) reduces public internet variance but you still have intra-cloud network hops. on-prem means you own the infra so you can tune connectivity, but you also take on operational responsibility. Dedicated with VPC peering gives a middle ground—Redwood's control plane still coordinates but dataplane is in dedicated pool.
[06:33] Rashid Khan: any notes on MTU and fragmentation? we saw odd latency when packets fragment.
[06:39] Priya Rao: set MTU to avoid fragmentation (9001 or proper path MTU), and ensure your VPC/VPN doesn't force 1500->1400 conversions. fragmentation leads to retransmits and long tail.
[06:48] [06:48] Tom Jenkins: do you have any recommended observability windows to capture p99 causes?
[06:53] Priya Rao: capture distributed traces (client, LB, edge, runtime), tcp metrics, kv cache hit/miss per request, batch size distribution, and s e r v e r queue depths. correlate spikes with autoscaler events. Redwood Console can show per-route latency breakdowns.
[07:08] Alex Martin: quick demo — Priya will show a small benchmark run against a staging Dedicated pool and we'll point out where p95 vs p99 comes from.
[07:16] Priya Rao: demo notes — this is a replay of sampling 10k requests generated from your prompt set, mix of streaming and non-streaming, with simulated VPC peering latency added.
[07:25] [07:25] Priya Rao: (screen) so here we have two charts: backend p95/p99 and e2e p95/p99. you can see the e2e p99 is ~350ms higher due to client TLS and a 3-hop peering path. backend p99 is 1.05s, e2e p99 ~1.4s.
[07:41] Maya Lopez: that aligns with our numbers. what's the typical improvement if we add a warm pool and pin sessions?
[07:46] Priya Rao: in our benchmarks warm pools and pinning reduced backend p99 by ~250-400ms for multi-turn workloads. again depends on prompt length.
[07:55] Alex Martin: and if you enable a low-latency route for your interactive traffic, you sacrifice some unit-cost efficiency but get tighter tail behavior.
[08:03] Tom Jenkins: curious about fallback strategies — if our main model is busy, can Redwood fallback to a smaller model gracefully?
[08:09] Priya Rao: yes, Redwood supports policy-based fallbacks and automatic downgrade to quantized or smaller variants for tail-preservation. you can configure quality thresholds to trigger fallbacks.
[08:22] Rashid Khan: what about measurement error — we've seen misaligned timestamps between our logs and Redwood's. how do we sync?
[08:29] Priya Rao: use NTP/chrony, and include request IDs in both logs. we recommend passing a unique request header (x-request-id) and Redwood will echo it so you can correlate traces.
[08:40] [08:40] Maya Lopez: can you also talk about kernel selection and how that affects tail?
[08:45] Priya Rao: kernel selection matters — some operations have variable latency depending on sequence length and batch composition. Redwood's runtime picks kernels optimized for typical seq len; outlier seq lengths can hit less-optimized codepaths causing jitter. We do per-model compilation and keep multiple kernels to reduce that effect.
[09:00] Alex Martin: ok shifting to concrete recommendations for Lighthouse: 1) run replay benchmark with your top-100 prompts, 2) enable warm pool + sticky routing for interactive route, 3) use streaming for TTF token improvement, 4) configure a low-latency route for interactive traffic and a cost route for batch jobs, 5) tune NAT/LB idle timeouts.
[09:18] Tom Jenkins: sounds good. what's the proposed timeline for a pilot?
[09:21] Alex Martin: we can spin up a 2-week Dedicated pilot starting next week if we get the traffic samples and VPC peering details. Priya will run the bench and share configs.
[09:29] Priya Rao: i'll prepare the benchmark config and runbook and share by monday. we'll also include instructions for client tcp/tls tuning and recommended keepalive settings.
[09:39] Maya Lopez: any security review items we should prep? we need SOC2 docs, data residency guarantees, and KMS integration notes.
[09:46] Alex Martin: we'll send SOC2 and ISO artifacts, plus a short note on KMS/HSM integration and audit logs.
[09:53] Rashid Khan: final thing — quantization: we want to run a quality smoke against our eval set before switching in production. can Redwood help automate that?
[10:00] Priya Rao: yes Redwood Optimize can run model/quantization regression checks against your eval prompts and surface quality regressions. we'll include that in the pilot run.
[10:10] [10:10] Tom Jenkins: great, appreciate the level of detail. any other Qs?
[10:15] Maya Lopez: one more: what about socket pool sizing on the client? any numbers?
[10:19] Priya Rao: depends on concurrency; for our workloads a pool of 50-100 keep-alive connections per host works well. we'll include tuned defaults.
[10:27] Alex Martin: ok recap of next steps — Priya sends benchmark + runbook; Alex sends pricing for 2-week Dedicated pilot and security artifacts; Tom sends prompt list and traffic profile; Maya coordinates VPC peering details with Rashid.
[10:41] Tom Jenkins: thanks all, we'll get those materials over.
[10:45] Alex Martin: thanks everyone, we'll follow up with calendar invites and the benchmark spreadsheet.
[10:50] End of recording.
